title: The write-ahead log: what it is and why everything else depends on it

videos.script: When PostgreSQL says COMMIT, your row is not in the table yet. {{commit}} It is in memory, on a page that has changed and not been written. If the power went now, that page would be gone. {{page}} And still the commit was honest, because the change was written somewhere else first: a log, appended to in order, and forced onto the disk before the answer came back. {{log}} That is the write-ahead log. Every change is described there before it touches a table file. The table files catch up later, in their own time. {{later}} This lesson opens the log. You will find your own row in it with grep, before it exists in the table. You will decode the records with pg_waldump, measure what one update costs, and watch a whole-page copy ride along with the first change after a checkpoint. {{waldump}} Then the part an administrator answers for. Crash recovery, replicas and backups all read this one log, and a single forgotten setting can make it grow until the disk is full. {{disk}}
